title: Titus 3:9–15
context: After the trustworthy saying Paul fences the church: shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; after a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a person who stirs up division. Travel plans, help for Zenas and Apollos, a charge that our people learn to maintain good works, and a closing greeting and grace.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on avoiding worthless controversy, a factious person after warning, and a people devoted to good works, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: An heretic (after a first and second admonition) reject—Avoid, leave to himself. Here it evidently means a man that obstinately persists in contending about foolish questions, and thereby occasions strife and parties in the church. And let ours—All our brethren at Crete. Learn—Both by thy admonition and example.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Titus 3:10, 14)

reformed.quote: He forbids him to waste much time in debating with heretics. Under this name he includes all ambitious, unruly, contentious persons who disturb the peace of the Church. After the first and second admonition. Let ours also learn to excel in good works, that they may not be unfruitful.

verses.text: but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
verses.arminianNotes:
But shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. The “but” sets this against the profitable good works of v. 8. Not every religious argument is obedience.

Controversy can be a way of resisting the mercy just preached. The Spirit enables a holy refusal of worthless talk; the church can still dive in and call it zeal. Profit is the test Paul just used: good works help people; these fights do not.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin will soon forbid wasting much time in debate with heretics. Here the catalog is foolish questions, genealogies, dissensions, legal quarrels—unprofitable and worthless. The trustworthy saying (v. 8) is not served by this diet.

God feeds His people on mercy and good works, not on speculative fights. Avoidance is obedience. The law-quarrels of Crete are not a higher spirituality; they are a substitute for the regeneration just described.

verses.text: Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning,
verses.arminianNotes:
Avoid a divisive man after a first and second warning. Wesley: an heretic, after a first and second admonition, reject—avoid, leave to himself. Here it means a man who obstinately persists in contending about foolish questions and thereby occasions strife and parties in the church.

Two warnings are means of grace; the person can still turn. After that, distance is also obedience. The aim is the church’s peace and the man’s conscience, not a taste for cutting people off. Persistence in party-making is treated as a settled refusal, not a personality quirk.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he forbids him to waste much time in debating with heretics. Under this name he includes all ambitious, unruly, contentious persons who disturb the peace of the Church. After the first and second admonition: then, in effect, be done.

Paul calls for patient warning first, then separation. God guards His flock by a limited debate, not by endless argument that treats strife as a gift. The factious person is not made the church’s tutor. Two admonitions honor both truth and patience; refusal after that is to be recognized, not endlessly managed.

verses.text: knowing that such a one is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned.
verses.arminianNotes:
Knowing that such a one is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned. The diagnosis is moral, not merely intellectual. He has judged himself by refusing the warnings.

A professing person can become warped by practiced division. Self-condemned names a responsibility he will not shift onto the church. The warnings of v. 10 were his door; remaining in the party is his verdict on himself. This is pastoral grief, not a sneer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Warped, sinful, self-condemned: Paul will not treat the factious as a misunderstood ally. The second warning having failed, the man’s own stance condemns him.

Persistent division after admonition is evidence of a heart not ruled by the trustworthy saying. Self-condemned means the church is not inventing the charge; he displays it. God keeps His people from being tutored by a man who has already passed sentence on himself.

verses.text: When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined to winter there.
verses.arminianNotes:
When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined to winter there. The letter lands in travel, winter, colleagues. Ministry is not only a doctrine chart.

Titus’s presence with Paul is a good work of companionship. Enabling grace includes showing up. The names remind Crete that the apostolic circle is larger than one young pastor on an island.
verses.reformedNotes:
Artemas or Tychicus will cover Crete so Titus can come to Nicopolis. Paul has decided to winter there. The mission has logistics because the Lord uses means: replacements, travel, a season.

God orders His servants’ steps, including wintering. The same mercy that saved (vv. 4–7) now steers an apostle’s calendar. Titus is not indispensable to Crete in a way that forbids him to come; the church is larger than one man.

verses.text: Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey speedily, that nothing may be lacking for them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey speedily. Hospitality is part of the good works just commanded. A lawyer and a preacher both need the church’s purse and haste.

“Nothing” is practical love. Grace that appeared for people trains people to fund the next mile. Neglect here would make the doctrine look cheap while controversies (v. 9) stay well fed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zenas and Apollos are to be sped on, lacking nothing. The church’s generosity is how God moves His workers. Apollos’s name ties Crete to the wider apostolic mission.

Provision for traveling servants is fruit of the regeneration already named. God does not scorn the purse. A justified people see that the laborers lack nothing, because the Savior who poured out the Spirit richly also cares for the journey.

verses.text: Let our people also learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let our people also learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful. Wesley: let ours—all our brethren at Crete—learn, both by thy admonition and example. Learning implies they might otherwise be unfruitful.

Our people are the household of faith, taught to meet urgent need. Good works are learned; they can be neglected. Fruitfulness is the opposite of the worthless controversies of v. 9. Mercy (vv. 4–7) is the root; urgent need is a reason the fruit must actually appear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: let ours also learn to excel in good works, that they may not be unfruitful. The same note as 3:8, now aimed at urgent need. “Our people” are the church in distinction from the factious.

God teaches a justified people to be fruitful. Learning is a means; unfruitfulness is not a harmless option for the regenerate. Urgent need is where the trustworthy saying becomes bread, escort, and care. Works remain fruit, not foundation.

verses.text: All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.
verses.arminianNotes:
All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with you all. The letter ends in affection and benediction. “You all” is as wide as the Cretan church Paul has been correcting and comforting.

Love in the faith is the family mark; grace with you all is the last word, not the controversies. The same grace that appeared for all people (2:11) and saved us by mercy (3:5) is now wished upon the whole church. Receive it; do not refuse it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Greetings from Paul’s company, and a greeting to those who love us in faith. Then: Grace be with you all. The apostle’s last word is the grace he has been preaching.

Those who love in the faith are the people Christ purified for Himself (2:14). Grace with you all is a benediction God means to apply to His church. The trustworthy saying ends as a blessing, not as a debate. The Lord who saved us according to mercy now greets His people through Paul’s mouth.
